extracted.subtask_description: States the foundational anticipation doctrine: a single reference must disclose every claim element, arranged as claimed, with strict identity (not mere similarity), plus the narrow exceptions for multi-reference use, range anticipation rules, and irrelevant rebuttals (secondary considerations, nonanalogous art, disparagement).

rubrics_metrics.name: Each and every element test
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim is unpatentable under 35 U.S.C. 102 as anticipated only when a single prior art reference discloses every element required by the claim, either expressly or inherently. "A claim is anticipated only if each and every element as set forth in the claim is found, either expressly or inherently described, in a single prior art reference." (*Verdegaal Bros. v. Union Oil Co.*, 814 F.2d 628, 631 (Fed. Cir. 1987).) This is a strict, mechanical test at the level of the individual claim limitation: partial disclosure, or disclosure that is "close" but omits one element, is not anticipation — it may only support an obviousness rejection under § 103. There is no room for a "gist" or overall-similarity comparison; the comparison must proceed limitation-by-limitation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Genus/alternative claims — any single instance within scope anticipates
rubrics_metrics.description: Where a claim reads generically or covers alternative structures/compositions, anticipation is established if any single structure or composition falling within the scope of the claim is found in the prior art (*Brown v. 3M*, 265 F.3d 1349, 1351 (Fed. Cir. 2001) — a generic/Markush-type limitation is anticipated by prior art disclosure of one instance within its scope).

rubrics_metrics.name: Identity of invention — the matching standard
rubrics_metrics.description: Anticipation requires strict identity, not mere overlap or similarity of function: "[T]he identical invention must be shown in as complete detail as is contained in the … claim." (*Richardson v. Suzuki Motor Co.*, 868 F.2d 1226, 1236 (Fed. Cir. 1989).) This "identical invention" language is the operative matching criterion examiners and practitioners use to separate anticipation (identity) from obviousness (difference bridged by motivation/reasoning). If the reference and the claim differ by even one limitation, § 102 does not apply regardless of how minor or predictable the difference is.

rubrics_metrics.name: "Arranged as in the claim" — structural/relational requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: Element identity alone is not sufficient: the elements disclosed in the reference must also be arranged, connected, or combined the same way the claim recites. A reference that discloses all the same components used in a different configuration does not anticipate. Not an *ipsissimis verbis* test — the reference need not use the same words as the claim; matching is a substantive comparison of structure/function, not a lexical string match (*In re Bond*, 910 F.2d 831, 833 (Fed. Cir. 1990)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical matching rule: every claim limitation must (a) be found in the single reference, and (b) be found standing in the same structural/functional relationship to the other disclosed elements that the claim recites. Finding all the "parts" scattered across a reference, without the claimed connectivity/arrangement, is not anticipation.

rubrics_metrics.name: "At once envisage" carve-out for un-spelled-out arrangements
rubrics_metrics.description: A reference can anticipate an arrangement it never spells out verbatim, if a skilled reader would "at once envisage" that specific arrangement from the reference's teaching (*Kennametal, Inc. v. Ingersoll Cutting Tool Co.*, 780 F.3d 1376, 1381 (Fed. Cir. 2015)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This gloss does not rescue a reference that is missing a limitation outright — it only resolves cases where the reference discloses a limited, closed set of possible combinations and the claimed combination is one of the small number a skilled artisan would immediately recognize as taught (*Nidec Motor Corp. v. Zhongshan Broad Ocean Motor Co.*, 851 F.3d 1270 (Fed. Cir. 2017)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Multiple-reference § 102 exceptions (§ 2131.01) — enablement, term meaning, inherency support
rubrics_metrics.description: The general rule is that anticipation rejections rely on a single reference. Three narrow situations permit an examiner to cite additional references without converting the rejection into obviousness, because the extra material does not supply a missing claim limitation: (A) to prove the primary reference's disclosure is enabling (*In re Samour*, 571 F.2d 559 (CCPA 1978); *In re Donohue*, 766 F.2d 531 (Fed. Cir. 1985)); (B) to explain the meaning of terms used in the primary reference, construing but not expanding them (*In re Baxter Travenol Labs.*, 952 F.2d 388 (Fed. Cir. 1991); *Actelion Pharmaceuticals Ltd v. Mylan Pharmaceuticals Inc.*, 85 F.4th 1167 (Fed. Cir. 2023)); (C) to show that a characteristic not explicitly disclosed is nonetheless inherent, where evidence makes clear the missing descriptive matter is necessarily present and would be recognized by skilled artisans (*Continental Can Co. USA v. Monsanto Co.*, 948 F.2d 1264, 1268 (Fed. Cir. 1991); *Atlas Powder Co. v. IRECO, Inc.*, 190 F.3d 1342, 1348-49 (Fed. Cir. 1999)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Anticipation of ranges — a single in-range point anticipates
rubrics_metrics.description: A single example within a claimed range anticipates the whole range: if a claim covers a genus of numerical values/compositions, disclosure of one specific point falling within that range anticipates the claim, even though the claim as a whole covers a broader range (*Titanium Metals Corp. v. Banner*, 778 F.2d 775 (Fed. Cir. 1985); *UCB, Inc. v. Actavis Labs. UT, Inc.*, 65 F.4th 679 (Fed. Cir. 2023)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Overlapping/touching ranges require case-by-case specificity analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Where the prior art discloses a range that touches or overlaps the claimed range, but does not give a specific example falling within the claimed sub-range, anticipation depends on whether the disclosure is specific enough to constitute anticipation of the narrower claimed range.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contrast: *ClearValue Inc. v. Pearl River Polymers Inc.*, 668 F.3d 1340 (Fed. Cir. 2012) — claimed alkalinity below 50 ppm was anticipated by a reference disclosing the process works for systems with alkalinity "150 ppm and less," because there was no evidence of criticality or difference in the claimed sub-range. *Atofina v. Great Lakes Chem. Corp.*, 441 F.3d 991 (Fed. Cir. 2006) — a reference's disclosed range of 100-500°C did not anticipate a claimed sub-range of 330-450°C, because "the disclosure of a range is no more a disclosure of the end points of the range than it is each of the intermediate points," and the patentee showed the claimed range was critical. When unclear, examiners may issue a combined 102/103 rejection (*Ex parte Lee*, 31 USPQ2d 1105 (Bd. Pat. App. & Inter. 1993)).

rubrics_metrics.name: A merely close, non-overlapping value never anticipates
rubrics_metrics.description: A value/range that is merely close, but does not overlap, never anticipates. Anticipation requires the reference to disclose "exactly what is claimed"; any gap between reference and claim — however small — must be addressed under § 103, not § 102 (*Titanium Metals Corp. v. Banner*, 778 F.2d 775 (Fed. Cir. 1985)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Secondary considerations are irrelevant to anticipation (§ 2131.04)
rubrics_metrics.description: Evidence of secondary considerations (unexpected results, commercial success, long-felt need, etc.) has no bearing on a § 102 anticipation rejection and cannot rebut it, because anticipation is a purely factual identity-of-disclosure question, not a question of obviousness-weighing (*In re Wiggins*, 488 F.2d 538, 543 (CCPA 1973)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Nonanalogous or disparaging prior art is still anticipatory (§ 2131.05)
rubrics_metrics.description: "Analogous art" is not a requirement for anticipation. Arguments that the reference is "nonanalogous art" or "teaches away" from the claimed invention are not germane to a § 102 rejection — these arguments matter only for obviousness (*In re Self*, 671 F.2d 1344, 1350-51 (CCPA 1982)). A reference may come from an entirely different field of endeavor and is nonetheless anticipatory so long as it explicitly or inherently discloses every claim limitation (*State Contracting & Eng'g Corp. v. Condotte America, Inc.*, 346 F.3d 1057, 1068 (Fed. Cir. 2003)). A reference that discloses the invention and then criticizes or disparages it is still anticipatory as to that disclosure (*Celeritas Technologies Ltd. v. Rockwell International Corp.*, 150 F.3d 1354, 1361 (Fed. Cir. 1998)).
